title: The table that predicted the future

probes.question: What did Mendeleev do with the gaps in his table?
options: Left them blank because the data was missing
Predicted that undiscovered elements would fill them
Filled them with copies of nearby elements

probes.question: True or false: gallium, discovered in 1875, closely matched Mendeleev's predicted eka-aluminium.

image.alt: A close-up of Dmitri Mendeleev's handwritten notes with elements and atomic weights crossed out and reworked.

panels.text: 1869. Dmitri Mendeleev arranges the elements by atomic mass and sees that their chemical properties follow a pattern.
Not every element was known, so his table had gaps. Instead of hiding them, he predicted that undiscovered elements would fill them.
He called one eka-aluminium, expecting an atomic mass of about 68 and a density of about 6.0 g/cm³. In 1875 Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium.
Gallium came out at about 69.7 and 5.91 g/cm³. In 1886 germanium, predicted as eka-silicon, matched too. The table was not just a list, it was a map with blanks.
